title: Four words from Race After Technology
introduction: In Week 5 we read Ruha Benjamin's Race After Technology (2019) in four groups. Each group took one chapter and one word, read for twenty minutes, and wrote a short definition on a shared pad. I was in Group 4, Technological Benevolence. This post is my glossary of all four words: the group definitions from the pad, one example from the book, and what I think.
related_work:
Glossary

1. Engineered Inequity (Chapter 1)

Group 1 wrote: Non-democratic systems, typically built by private companies, leave almost no room to question the biases embedded within algorithmic systems; embedding human biases into algorithms is an extremely harmful practice. They also quoted this passage from the book: ‘The way we conceive of our relationship with robots holds up a mirror for us to reflect upon and challenge the concept of “race as technology”.’

The book states: inequality is not an accidental by-product of technology, but is designed into it. Human biases and social hierarchies are encoded into systems and subsequently presented as objective facts. Benjamin cites an example: a 2016 beauty pageant judged by an algorithm, in which nearly all of the 44 winners were white.

My view: In most cases, AI image generators still operate on the basis of stereotypes. Ask it to generate a Middle Eastern man, and you get a face with a full beard and a headscarf; ask it to generate a Middle Eastern woman, and you get an image of someone wearing a headscarf and a veil. Training data and design choices transform stereotypes into ‘what these people look like’, and the output only appears neutral because it is generated by a machine.

2. Default Discrimination (Chapter 2)

Group 2 wrote: Even if no one intends it, technology can still treat certain people unfairly. Police software uses outdated data, and as a result, police resources are continually directed towards neighbourhoods with large Black populations. People refer to this as a ‘system error’, but this precisely demonstrates that the system itself is unfair; algorithms not only make mistakes, but also replicate existing inequalities and make them appear objective and reasonable.

The book states: ‘Default’ refers to factory settings. Nobody presses a button labelled ‘discrimination’, but the system learns from past data, and since the past itself is unequal, the system will generate discrimination on its own if left unchecked. Predictive policing is a case in point: the more arrests a neighbourhood has seen in the past, the greater the police presence there is now, which in turn leads to more arrests, creating a vicious circle.

My view: In our daily lives, the default settings of the apps we use are precisely this kind of ‘default’ state. Beauty filters have already made your face slimmer and your skin fairer before you’ve even had a chance to adjust them. Translation software will translate ‘doctor’ as ‘he’ and ‘nurse’ as ‘she’. There is a great deal of overlap between the content of Chapters One and Two; for me, the distinction lies in the fact that engineered inequity is deliberately designed, whilst default discrimination arises of its own accord when no one is paying attention.

3. Coded Exposure (Chapter 3)

Group 3 wrote: Computers may be biased; some people receive excessive attention, whilst others are overlooked. Certain sensors do not function properly with Black people, yet the companies concerned have failed to rectify this.

The book states: Technology creates inequality in the perception of people in two ways. Certain groups are overexposed, monitored by cameras and facial recognition systems wherever they go; whilst other groups are underexposed, rendering them virtually invisible to machines: Kodak film was calibrated for fair skin tones, so darker skin appeared as shadows in photographs; later facial tracking technology was also unable to track Black faces. Both situations cause harm. In class, Miha added: do not stop at the superficial phenomenon of ‘sensor malfunction’; instead, probe deeper to understand the cause; the sensor was originally designed around the light-reflective properties of fair skin.

My view: I cannot find a similar example from my own experience, and perhaps that is precisely the crux of the matter. Technology has always been able to identify me accurately, so I have never been aware of this issue. This ‘unnoticed’ status is precisely the privilege enjoyed by those who are ‘seen’.

4. Technological Benevolence (Chapter 4, ‘Do Fixes Fix Us?’)

This was my group’s word. We wrote: Technology designed to help people may still exacerbate inequality; good intentions do not guarantee fair outcomes, particularly when technological solutions fail to address deeper-rooted social issues.

Case study from the book: ‘Diversity Inc.’ claims to help businesses ‘serve and include’ different ethnic groups. As the law prohibits the direct collection of racial data, the company infers your ethnicity based on your name and postcode, then sells this label to insurance, property and pharmaceutical companies. Whilst this appears to be helping ethnic minorities integrate into society, it is in fact exploiting their identity for profit. Benjamin refers to this as ‘racial capitalism’. On the surface, it is altruism; at its core, it is poison.

My view: These technologies appear well-intentioned on the surface. They claim to help people, eliminate bias or promote the inclusion of minority groups. Yet harm is often concealed behind this benevolence. The focus of this chapter is not on eliminating bias, but on seeing through this veneer of ‘goodwill’ to uncover the prejudice that still persists. Change is difficult because some people profit from this ‘correction’, and so it will not disappear.
results_discussion:
Take me as an example: I chose disposable e-cigarettes because I had been using them all along. They are marketed as a ‘solution’: a way to quit smoking that is less harmful to the body and less harmful to the environment. But after using them, I found the reality to be quite the opposite. They are more addictive, remain highly harmful to the body, and the small batteries discarded everywhere are even harder to recycle than cigarette butts. The so-called ‘solution’ is, in reality, simply the thrill of nicotine. E-cigarettes are a ‘solution’ that keeps you ‘stuck’ where you are. I have distilled three questions from this chapter: Who benefits from this? Who foots the bill? And who is left ‘stuck’ in their current situation?

In the latter half of the lecture, Miha shifted the focus from the book to resource extraction: the cobalt in every screen, the mines in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the assembly lines behind them, and what Neema Iyer terms ‘digital extractivism’. This mirrors the supply chain of disposable e-cigarettes to a tee, and it is precisely the core of my artistic practice.
